issues.explanation: The trigger 'Arab villages' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of physical abuse by a romantic partner and the rest of the profile, which centers on interpersonal abuse-related cues, self-appraisals, and memory phenomena. Without any corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal content involving war, military, or ethnic/geographic conflict, this item appears clinically incoherent for this patient.

issues.item: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Strictly restricting eating to feel in control is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other selected items coherently describe PTSD related to partner physical abuse (criticism, violence, offender cues; fragmented/alien memory; rage; dehumanization, self-blame, emotional numbing; distraction and cue avoidance). In contrast, restrictive eating introduces a distinct control-focused coping pattern that is not reflected elsewhere in triggers, memory, threat, or appraisals, making it clinically hard to explain as part of the same formulation rather than a separate problem.

vignette: Kanalu had always been a meticulous editor, known for his keen eye and sharp instincts. But after the abuse he suffered at the hands of his ex-partner, he began to doubt his own judgment. The slightest criticism from a colleague or author would send him reeling, his mind racing with thoughts of inadequacy. He couldn't shake the feeling that he was somehow to blame for the violence he had endured. The memories of those moments still felt like snapshots in his mind - vivid, but disconnected from his own experience. When he recalled the sound of his partner's voice, raised in anger, or the feel of a blow landing on his skin, Kanalu would feel a surge of rage course through his body. It was as if his emotions were trapped in those frozen moments, unable to move forward. As time passed, Kanalu found himself avoiding anything that might trigger those memories. He stopped going to writing groups, where he had once thrived on the feedback and camaraderie. He turned down social invitations, afraid of being drawn into conversations that might veer too close to his past. Even reading certain authors or genres became off-limits, as they reminded him too much of his ex-partner's tastes. At work, Kanalu began to withdraw from his colleagues. He stopped offering suggestions or critiques, fearing that his opinions would be met with scorn. His usual attention to detail started to slip, and he found himself distracted by the smallest things - a misplaced comma, a poorly formatted paragraph. It was as if he had lost his sense of purpose, his confidence shattered by the abuse. Kanalu's isolation deepened when he realized that even his own emotions were off-limits. He couldn't allow himself to feel anything too strongly, lest it bring back those overwhelming memories. He felt like an object, a shell of his former self, rather than a person with thoughts and feelings. The worst part was the sense of shame that lingered long after the abuse had ended. Kanalu couldn't shake the feeling that he was somehow responsible for what had happened - that there was something fundamentally flawed about him, something that had invited the violence into his life. It was as if he had lost touch with his own identity, and was now just a shadow of the person he once was. It wasn't until Kanalu received an invitation to edit a book on domestic violence that he realized how much his avoidance had cost him. The topic hit too close to home, but it also sparked something within him - a desire to confront the demons he had been running from for so long. With a sense of trepidation, Kanalu decided to seek help, hoping that therapy might be the first step towards reclaiming his life and rediscovering himself.
